tool.name: Rust
tool.tagline: Fast, memory-safe systems language with no garbage collector
tool.description: Rust is a compiled systems programming language that guarantees memory and thread safety at compile time through ownership and borrowing, without a garbage collector. It is used for command-line tools, web services, embedded firmware, WebAssembly, and performance-critical parts of browsers, operating systems and cloud infrastructure. Learning it teaches you to reason precisely about ownership, lifetimes and concurrency.

concepts.name: Cargo and your first program
concepts.summary: Install Rust with rustup, create a project with cargo new, and build and run it with cargo run.
concepts.why: Cargo is how every Rust project is built, run, tested and shared, so it is the first tool you touch.
concepts.body:
Rust is installed with **rustup**, which manages toolchains (`stable`, `beta`, `nightly`) and keeps them updated with `rustup update`. It also installs `rustc`, the compiler, and **Cargo**, the build tool and package manager. In practice you almost never call `rustc` directly.

`cargo new hello` creates a package: a `Cargo.toml` manifest and `src/main.rs`. The manifest names the package, sets `edition = "2024"` (the language edition, which controls a few syntax and lint defaults) and lists dependencies.

The everyday commands:

- `cargo run` compiles in debug mode and runs the binary.
- `cargo build --release` builds an optimized binary into `target/release/`. Debug builds are fast to compile but can be 10-50x slower at runtime, so always benchmark release builds.
- `cargo check` type-checks without producing a binary. It is much faster, so use it constantly while editing.
- `cargo fmt` formats code and `cargo clippy` runs the linter; both are standard in real projects.

Every binary starts at `fn main()`. `println!` is a **macro** (note the `!`), which is how Rust supports format strings that are checked at compile time. Placeholders are `{}` for user-facing `Display` output and `{:?}` for `Debug` output, and you can put variable names inline: `println!("{name}")`.

The compiler's error messages are unusually good. Read them fully: they usually point at the exact span and often suggest the fix.
takeaways: `cargo new`, `cargo run`, `cargo check`, `cargo build --release` cover daily work
`{}` uses Display, `{:?}` uses Debug; names can go inline as `{name}`
Measure performance only on release builds
pitfalls: Benchmarking a debug build and concluding Rust is slow.

quiz.q: You are iterating on code and only want to know whether it compiles. Which command is fastest?
quiz.explain: cargo check runs type and borrow checking but skips code generation, so it is the quickest feedback loop.

concepts.name: Variables and mutability
concepts.summary: Bind values with let, opt into mutation with mut, and use shadowing and const where they fit.
concepts.why: Immutability by default is the first place Rust pushes you toward code that is easier to reason about.
concepts.body:
`let` introduces a binding. Bindings are **immutable by default**: once `let x = 5;` runs, assigning `x = 6` is a compile error. To allow changes, say so with `let mut x = 5;`. This makes every place that mutates state visible at the declaration.

Types are inferred from usage, so annotations are optional in most local code: `let count: u32 = 0;` is the same as `let count = 0u32;`. When inference cannot decide (for example parsing a string), the compiler asks you to annotate.

**Shadowing** means declaring a new variable with the same name: `let x = x + 1;`. Unlike `mut`, it creates a fresh binding, so you can even change the type, which is handy for transforming input step by step (`let input = input.trim();`). The old value still exists until the end of its scope but is no longer reachable by that name.

`const` declares a compile-time constant. It always needs a type, is written in `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`, and can live at module level: `const MAX_USERS: usize = 1_000;`. A `static` is similar but has one fixed memory address for the whole program; prefer `const` unless you need that address.

A binding must be initialised before use, but not necessarily at the `let`: the compiler tracks definite initialisation, so `let x; if c { x = 1 } else { x = 2 }` is fine. Unused variables produce warnings; prefix them with `_` to silence the warning on purpose.
takeaways: Bindings are immutable unless declared `let mut`
Shadowing creates a new binding and may change the type
`const` needs a type annotation and is evaluated at compile time
pitfalls: Reaching for `mut` when shadowing (a transformed, immutable value) expresses the intent better.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between `let x = x * 2;` (shadowing) and `x = x * 2;` on a `let mut x`?
options: Shadowing creates a new binding, which may have a different type
Shadowing is only allowed inside loops
Shadowing mutates the original memory in place
There is no difference after compilation, so the compiler treats them identically
quiz.explain: Shadowing introduces a brand-new variable that happens to reuse the name, so its type may differ; assignment to a `mut` binding must keep the type.

concepts.name: Scalar and compound types
concepts.summary: Integers, floats, bool and char, plus tuples and fixed-size arrays, and how Rust handles overflow and conversions.
concepts.why: Rust never converts numbers implicitly, so knowing the primitive types saves you from most early compile errors.
concepts.body:
Rust has four **scalar** types. Integers come in signed `i8` to `i128` and unsigned `u8` to `u128`, plus `isize`/`usize`, which are pointer-sized; `usize` is the type of indices and lengths. The default integer is `i32`, the default float is `f64` (`f32` also exists). `bool` is `true`/`false`, and `char` is a 4-byte Unicode scalar value written `'a'` or `'é'`, not a byte.

There are **no implicit conversions**. Adding an `i32` to a `u64` is a compile error; convert explicitly with `as` (which truncates or wraps silently) or with `From`/`TryFrom` (`u8::try_from(300)` returns an `Err`). Prefer `try_from` when a value might not fit.

Integer overflow panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds. When wrapping or saturation is what you mean, say so: `wrapping_add`, `saturating_sub`, `checked_mul` (returns `Option`).

Two built-in **compound** types group values:

- A **tuple** `(i32, &str, bool)` holds a fixed number of values of different types. Access fields with `t.0`, `t.1`, or destructure with `let (a, b, c) = t;`. The empty tuple `()`, called unit, is what functions return when they return nothing.
- An **array** `[u8; 4]` holds a fixed number of values of one type on the stack. `[0; 256]` repeats a value. Indexing is bounds-checked: `arr[10]` on a 4-element array panics instead of reading random memory.

For a growable list you will use `Vec<T>`, covered later.
takeaways: Default numeric types are `i32` and `f64`; `usize` is for indices and lengths
No implicit numeric conversions: use `as`, `From` or `TryFrom`
Overflow panics in debug and wraps in release unless you use the explicit methods
Tuples mix types; arrays have a fixed length and bounds-checked indexing
pitfalls: Using `as` for narrowing conversions and silently truncating values; use `try_from` when it might not fit.

quiz.q: What does `300_i32 as u8` evaluate to?
quiz.explain: `as` between integers truncates to the low bits: 300 mod 256 = 44, with no error or panic.

quiz.q: Which type is used for vector and array indices?
quiz.explain: Indexing and lengths use `usize`, which is as wide as a pointer on the target.

concepts.name: Functions and expressions
concepts.summary: Declare functions with typed parameters and return values, and understand why almost everything in Rust is an expression.
concepts.why: Knowing that blocks are expressions explains Rust's missing `return` statements and stray-semicolon errors.
concepts.body:
Functions are declared with `fn`, parameters always carry explicit types, and the return type follows `->`. Type inference works inside function bodies but never across signatures, which keeps signatures readable as documentation.

Rust is **expression-oriented**. A block `{ ... }` evaluates to its last expression, if that expression has no trailing semicolon. That is how functions return values without `return`:

```rust
fn square(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x * x
}
```

Adding a semicolon (`x * x;`) turns the expression into a statement, the block then evaluates to `()`, and you get a "mismatched types: expected `i32`, found `()`" error. Recognise this one; everyone hits it.

`return` still exists and is used for **early** exits, for example a guard at the top of a function. `if`, `match` and blocks are expressions too, so you can write `let label = if n > 0 { "pos" } else { "non-pos" };`. Both branches must then have the same type.

A function with no `->` returns `()`. A function that never returns, such as one that always panics or loops forever, can be declared `-> !` (the never type).

Function names use `snake_case`. Order does not matter: you can call a function defined further down the file. Rust has no default arguments or overloading; use different names, an `Option` parameter, or a builder struct instead.
takeaways: Parameter and return types are always written out
The last expression of a block, without `;`, is its value
`return` is for early exits; `if` and `match` are expressions
pitfalls: Ending the final line with `;` and getting `expected i32, found ()`.

quiz.q: What does `fn f() -> i32 { 5; }` produce?
options: A compile error: the body evaluates to () not i32
A warning only, and it returns 5
quiz.explain: The semicolon turns `5` into a statement, so the block's value is `()`, which does not match `i32`.

concepts.name: Control flow: if, loop, while, for
concepts.summary: Branch with if, repeat with loop, while and for over ranges, and use labels and break values.
concepts.why: Loops and branches are everyday tools, and Rust's versions are expressions with a few useful twists.
concepts.body:
`if` conditions must be a `bool`; there is no truthiness, so `if count { }` on an integer does not compile. Write `if count != 0`. As an expression, `if`/`else` can produce a value as long as both arms have the same type.

Rust has three loops:

- `loop { }` repeats forever until `break`. It is an expression: `break value` makes the loop evaluate to `value`, which is a neat way to retry until something succeeds.
- `while cond { }` runs while a condition holds.
- `for item in iterable { }` walks anything iterable. It is the most common loop and avoids index bugs.

Ranges drive counting loops: `0..5` is 0 to 4, `0..=5` includes 5, and `(0..5).rev()` counts down. To loop over a collection without consuming it, borrow it: `for x in &items`. Use `for (i, x) in items.iter().enumerate()` when you also need the index, instead of indexing manually.

Nested loops can be **labelled** with a lifetime-like name, `'outer: for ...`, so that `break 'outer` or `continue 'outer` targets the outer loop.

Since Rust 1.88 the 2024 edition also allows **let chains** in `if` and `while`: `if let Some(x) = opt && x > 10 { }`. You will meet `if let` with `Option` shortly.

There is no C-style `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` loop and no `++` operator; use ranges and `+= 1`.
takeaways: Conditions must be `bool`; there is no truthiness
`for x in &collection` and ranges like `0..n` replace index loops
`loop` can return a value with `break value`; labels target outer loops
pitfalls: Writing `for x in vec` and then being surprised the vector was moved; use `&vec` to borrow.

quiz.q: How many times does the body of `for i in 0..=3 {}` run?
quiz.explain: `0..=3` is an inclusive range: 0, 1, 2, 3, so four iterations.

quiz.q: What value does `let v = loop { break 7; };` give `v`?
options: It does not compile because loop cannot be assigned
quiz.explain: `loop` is an expression and `break 7` makes it evaluate to 7.

concepts.name: Ownership and moves
concepts.summary: Every value has one owner; assignment moves ownership, and the value is freed when its owner goes out of scope.
concepts.why: Ownership is the idea that gives Rust memory safety without a garbage collector; everything else builds on it.
concepts.body:
Rust manages memory with three rules: each value has exactly one **owner** (a variable or a field); there is one owner at a time; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is **dropped** and its resources are freed. No garbage collector, no manual `free`.

Consider `String`, which owns a heap buffer. `let s2 = s1;` does not copy the buffer. It **moves** ownership to `s2`, and `s1` becomes unusable; using it afterwards is a compile error ("borrow of moved value"). If both stayed valid, both would try to free the same buffer at scope end. Passing a value to a function moves it too, and returning a value moves it out to the caller.

When you really want a second independent copy, call `.clone()`. Clones are explicit precisely because they can be expensive, so they are easy to spot in review.

Small types that live entirely on the stack, such as integers, floats, `bool`, `char` and tuples or arrays of them, implement **`Copy`**. Assigning them copies the bits, and the original stays usable. Anything that owns a heap resource (`String`, `Vec`, `Box`) is not `Copy`.

Moves are checked at compile time: the compiler tracks, per path through your code, whether a variable may have been moved. A variable moved in only one branch of an `if` is treated as moved afterwards.

Constantly moving values in and out of functions would be tedious, which is why the next lesson introduces borrowing.
takeaways: Each value has a single owner and is dropped when the owner goes out of scope
Assignment and passing by value move non-`Copy` types
`.clone()` makes an explicit deep copy; simple scalars are `Copy`
pitfalls: Sprinkling `.clone()` everywhere to silence the borrow checker instead of borrowing.

quiz.q: After `let v = vec![1, 2]; let w = v;`, what happens if you use `v`?
options: It works, both point to the same vector
It works, w is a deep copy
quiz.explain: `Vec` is not `Copy`, so the assignment moves ownership to `w` and the compiler rejects later uses of `v`.

quiz.q: Which of these types is `Copy`?
quiz.explain: A tuple of `Copy` types is `Copy`; the others own heap memory and are moved.

concepts.name: References and borrowing
concepts.summary: Lend access with & and &mut references, and learn the rule: many readers or one writer, never both.
concepts.why: Borrowing is how you use values without taking ownership, and its rules are what the borrow checker enforces.
concepts.body:
A **reference** lets you use a value without owning it. `&s` creates a shared reference; a function taking `&String` (or better, `&str`) can read the string, and the caller keeps ownership. This is called **borrowing**.

To modify through a reference, both the binding and the reference must be mutable: `let mut s = ...; change(&mut s);` with `fn change(s: &mut String)`.

The core rule the **borrow checker** enforces: at any point, you may have either any number of shared references (`&T`) or exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`) to a value, never both. This rules out data races and iterator-invalidation bugs at compile time: you cannot push to a `Vec` while holding a reference to one of its elements, because the push might reallocate.

References must also never outlive what they point to. Returning `&String` to a local variable is rejected, because the local is dropped when the function returns. (Return the owned `String` instead.)

Borrows last only until their **last use**, not until the end of the block. This is called non-lexical lifetimes, and it is why code like "take `&v[0]`, print it, then `v.push(4)`" compiles: the shared borrow ended at the print.

The `.` operator auto-references and auto-dereferences, so `s.len()` works whether `s` is a `String`, `&String` or `&mut String`. For other operations, `*r` dereferences explicitly, for example `*count += 1` through a `&mut i32`.
takeaways: `&T` borrows for reading, `&mut T` for writing; the owner keeps ownership
Many `&T` or one `&mut T` at a time, never both
A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the block
pitfalls: Holding a reference into a `Vec` across a `push`; the compiler rejects it because the push may reallocate.

quiz.q: Why does Rust reject taking `&mut v` while a `&v[0]` is still used later?
options: Mutable and shared borrows of the same value may not overlap
Only one reference of any kind is allowed
quiz.explain: Overlapping `&` and `&mut` borrows could let the mutation invalidate the shared reference, so the borrow checker forbids it.

concepts.name: Slices and string slices
concepts.summary: Borrow part of an array, Vec or String as a slice (&[T] or &str) and write functions that accept any of them.
concepts.why: Taking slices instead of owned collections makes your functions both cheaper and more flexible.
concepts.body:
A **slice** is a borrowed view into a contiguous sequence: a pointer plus a length. `&[T]` views elements of an array or `Vec<T>`, and `&str` views UTF-8 bytes of a `String` or string literal. Slices do not own anything, so they follow the borrowing rules.

Create them with range syntax: `&v[1..3]` (elements 1 and 2), `&v[..2]`, `&v[2..]`, `&v[..]`. Out-of-range bounds panic.

String literals like `"hello"` have type `&'static str`: a slice pointing into the program binary, valid for the whole run.

The most useful habit is in function signatures. Prefer:

- `&str` over `&String`,
- `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>`.

Thanks to **deref coercion**, a `&String` automatically converts to `&str` and a `&Vec<T>` to `&[T]`, so the slice version accepts strictly more callers, including literals and arrays.

Because a slice borrows from its source, the compiler keeps the source alive and unmodified while the slice is in use. A classic example: if a function returns `&str` pointing at the first word of a `String`, you cannot `clear()` the string while still using that word.

One gotcha: string slice indices are **byte** offsets. Slicing in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character, like `&"héllo"[0..2]`, panics at runtime. When working with text, prefer methods such as `split_whitespace`, `find` or `char_indices` that return valid boundaries.

`&mut [T]` is the mutable counterpart, letting you modify elements in place (for example `slice.sort()`), though it cannot change the length.
takeaways: A slice is a borrowed pointer + length: `&[T]` or `&str`
Accept `&str` and `&[T]` in signatures; `&String` and `&Vec` coerce to them
String slice indices are byte offsets and must land on char boundaries
pitfalls: Slicing text by byte index and panicking on non-ASCII characters.

quiz.q: Which parameter type accepts a `String`, a string literal and a `&str` from elsewhere?
quiz.explain: A `&String` coerces to `&str` and literals already are `&str`, so `&str` covers all three.

concepts.name: Structs and methods
concepts.summary: Group named fields into a struct, attach methods and associated functions in impl blocks, and pick the right self.
concepts.why: Structs are how you model your domain, and impl blocks are where most Rust code lives.
concepts.body:
A **struct** groups named fields into a new type. Instantiate it by naming every field; the field init shorthand lets you write `User { name, active: true }` when a variable has the same name as the field. **Struct update syntax** `User { active: false, ..other }` fills the rest from another value (moving any non-`Copy` fields out of it).

Rust also has **tuple structs** `struct Meters(f64);`, useful as lightweight wrappers (the newtype pattern) that stop you from mixing up a `Meters` and a `Seconds`, and **unit structs** `struct Marker;` with no fields.

Behaviour goes in an `impl` block. The first parameter decides how a method uses the value:

- `&self` reads it (most methods),
- `&mut self` modifies it,
- `self` consumes it, typically to transform it into something else.

Functions in an `impl` block without a `self` parameter are **associated functions**, called with `Type::name()`. By convention a constructor is `fn new(...) -> Self`. `Self` is an alias for the type being implemented.

Fields are private outside the module that defines the struct unless marked `pub`. Keeping fields private and exposing methods lets you maintain invariants, such as "width is never negative".

`#[derive(Debug)]` above the struct lets you print it with `{:?}` or, pretty-printed, `{:#?}`. You will meet more derivable traits later.

Method calls auto-borrow: `rect.area()` turns into `Rectangle::area(&rect)` automatically, so you rarely write `&` at a call site.
takeaways: Methods take `&self`, `&mut self` or `self` depending on how they use the value
Associated functions like `new` have no `self` and are called with `Type::new`
Tuple structs make cheap newtypes; `#[derive(Debug)]` enables `{:?}`
pitfalls: Taking `self` by value in a method that only reads, which consumes the caller's struct.

quiz.q: A method should modify the struct but the caller must keep using it. Which receiver fits?
quiz.explain: `&mut self` borrows mutably, so the method can change fields and the caller keeps ownership.

concepts.name: Enums and match
concepts.summary: Model values that can be one of several variants, each with its own data, and handle every case with match.
concepts.why: Enums with data plus exhaustive match are Rust's main tool for making invalid states unrepresentable.
concepts.body:
An **enum** defines a type whose value is exactly one of several **variants**. Unlike enums in C or Java, each variant can carry its own data: none, a tuple of values, or named fields.

```rust
enum Shape {
    Circle { radius: f64 },
    Rect(f64, f64),
    Empty,
}
```

You create a value with `Shape::Rect(2.0, 3.0)`, and you can add methods in an `impl` block just like with structs.

**`match`** compares a value against patterns from top to bottom and runs the first arm that matches. Patterns can destructure a variant and bind its data to names. `match` is **exhaustive**: if you forget a variant, the program does not compile. That is a big deal in practice: when you add a variant later, the compiler lists every `match` that must handle it.

The `_` pattern matches anything and is the catch-all. Use it deliberately, because it also silences the helpful exhaustiveness errors when new variants are added.

`match` is an expression, so all arms must produce the same type, and you can assign its result directly. Arms are separated by commas; a block arm `{ ... }` can hold several statements.

When matching on a reference (`match &shape`), patterns bind references to the inner data automatically, so you can inspect a value without moving out of it.

This style of data, called a sum type or tagged union, is used everywhere in Rust: messages, states of a state machine, AST nodes, and the standard `Option` and `Result` types.
takeaways: Each enum variant can carry different data
`match` is exhaustive: every variant must be handled
Avoid `_` catch-alls where you want the compiler to flag new variants
pitfalls: Using a struct with many optional fields and a `kind` string where an enum would make illegal states impossible.

quiz.q: You add a variant `Triangle` to `Shape`. What happens to an existing `match` that lists every variant without `_`?
options: It silently skips Triangle at runtime
It panics when it sees a Triangle
It fails to compile until Triangle is handled
It falls through to the first arm
quiz.explain: `match` must be exhaustive, so the compiler reports the missing `Triangle` arm.

concepts.name: Option, if let and let-else
concepts.summary: Represent a value that may be absent with Option<T>, and unpack it with match, if let, let-else and combinators.
concepts.why: Rust has no null; Option is how every API says 'maybe there is nothing here', so you use it constantly.
concepts.body:
Rust has no `null`. A value that may be missing has type **`Option<T>`**, a standard enum with two variants: `Some(T)` and `None`. Because `Option<i32>` and `i32` are different types, you cannot accidentally use a maybe-missing value as if it were there; the compiler makes you handle `None`.

You will meet it everywhere: `v.get(i)`, `map.get(&k)`, `s.find('x')`, `iter.next()` all return `Option`.

Ways to get at the value, from most to least explicit:

- `match opt { Some(x) => ..., None => ... }` handles both cases.
- `if let Some(x) = opt { ... }` handles only the case you care about, optionally with `else`.
- `let Some(x) = opt else { return; };` (**let-else**) binds `x` for the rest of the function and requires the `else` block to diverge (return, break, continue or panic). It keeps the happy path unindented.
- Combinators transform without unpacking: `opt.map(|x| x * 2)`, `opt.unwrap_or(0)`, `opt.unwrap_or_default()`, `opt.and_then(f)`, `opt.filter(...)`, and `opt.ok_or(err)` to convert into a `Result`.

`unwrap()` returns the value or panics on `None`; `expect("msg")` does the same with a message. They are fine in tests, prototypes, or when an invariant guarantees a value, but not for input that can legitimately be missing.

In the 2024 edition, let chains combine these: `if let Some(u) = user && u.active { ... }`.

To look inside an `Option<String>` without moving it, use `opt.as_deref()` (gives `Option<&str>`) or match on `&opt`.
takeaways: `Option<T>` replaces null; the type system forces you to handle `None`
`if let` for one case, `let ... else` for an early exit, combinators for transformations
`unwrap`/`expect` panic on `None`; keep them for true invariants and tests
pitfalls: Calling `.unwrap()` on user-controlled data and crashing on the first missing value.

quiz.q: What does `Some(3).map(|x| x + 1).unwrap_or(0)` return?
quiz.explain: `map` turns `Some(3)` into `Some(4)`, and `unwrap_or` extracts 4 because it is not `None`.

quiz.q: What must the `else` block of a `let Some(x) = opt else { ... };` do?
options: Return a default value for x
Diverge, e.g. return, break or panic
quiz.explain: let-else requires the else branch to never continue normally, since `x` would otherwise be unbound.

concepts.name: Patterns and destructuring
concepts.summary: Use patterns everywhere: destructure structs and tuples, add guards, match ranges, and bind with @.
concepts.why: Patterns appear in let, match, function parameters and loops; fluency with them makes Rust code short and clear.
concepts.body:
A **pattern** describes the shape of a value and binds parts of it to names. You have already used them in `match` and `if let`, but they also appear in `let`, `for`, `while let` and function parameters.

Destructuring:

- Tuples: `let (x, y) = point;`, `for (k, v) in &map`.
- Structs: `let User { name, age, .. } = user;` where `..` ignores the remaining fields.
- Slices: `match xs { [] => ..., [one] => ..., [first, .., last] => ... }`.
- Function parameters: `fn dist(&(x, y): &(f64, f64))`.

In a `match`, patterns can combine alternatives with `|` (`1 | 2 => ...`), match ranges (`'a'..='z'` or `0..=9`), and add a **match guard** with `if`: `Some(n) if n > 100 => ...`. A guard is checked after the pattern matches; if false, matching continues with the next arm. Note that the compiler does not consider guards when checking exhaustiveness, so you often still need a final arm.

The `@` operator binds a name while also testing a pattern: `n @ 1..=9 => println!("digit {n}")`.

`_` ignores one value without binding it; `_name` binds but suppresses the unused warning; `..` ignores the rest.

Patterns in `let` must be **irrefutable** (always match), like a tuple. Patterns that can fail, like `Some(x)`, need `if let`, `while let`, `let ... else` or `match`.

Matching on a reference binds references to the parts (called default binding modes), so `match &user` lets you look at fields without moving them. Use `ref`/`ref mut` only in the rare cases this does not cover.
takeaways: Patterns work in `let`, `match`, `if let`, `while let`, `for` and parameters
Use `|`, ranges, `..`, guards and `@` to express matches precisely
`let` needs irrefutable patterns; refutable ones need `if let`, `let-else` or `match`
pitfalls: Expecting the compiler to treat guarded arms as exhaustive; it never does.

quiz.q: Given `match n { x if x < 0 => "neg", 0 => "zero" }` on an i32, why does it fail to compile?
options: Guards are not allowed with integers
Positive numbers are not covered, and guards do not count toward exhaustiveness
quiz.explain: Positive values match no arm; the compiler requires a catch-all such as `_ => "pos"`.

concepts.name: Result and the ? operator
concepts.summary: Return Result<T, E> from fallible functions and propagate errors with ?, keeping panics for bugs.
concepts.why: Every I/O, parsing and network call returns Result; handling it fluently is the core of practical Rust.
concepts.body:
Rust separates two kinds of failure. **Unrecoverable** errors are bugs (an index out of range, a broken invariant) and trigger a `panic!`, which unwinds the thread. **Recoverable** errors, like a missing file or bad input, are ordinary values of type **`Result<T, E>`**, an enum with `Ok(T)` and `Err(E)`.

You can `match` on a `Result`, but the idiomatic way to pass errors up is the **`?` operator**. Inside a function that returns a `Result`, `let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;` means: if `Ok`, unwrap the value; if `Err`, return it from the current function immediately. Before returning, `?` converts the error with `From::from`, so a function returning `Result<T, MyError>` can use `?` on any error type that `MyError` implements `From` for. `?` also works on `Option` in functions returning `Option`.

`main` can return `Result<(), E>` where `E: Debug`; returning `Err` prints the error and exits with a non-zero code. A convenient quick signature is `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>`, since any standard error converts into that box.

Useful methods: `map_err` to change the error type, `ok()` to turn it into an `Option`, `unwrap_or_else`, `and_then`, and `is_ok()`/`is_err()`. `unwrap()` and `expect()` panic on `Err`.

`Result` is marked `#[must_use]`, so ignoring one produces a warning. If you really do not care, write `let _ = do_thing();` to show it was deliberate.

A good rule: library code returns `Result` and lets the caller decide; only application code at the top decides to print, retry or exit.
takeaways: Panics are for bugs; `Result` is for failures the caller should handle
`?` returns early on `Err` and converts the error with `From`
`main` can return `Result` to use `?` at the top level
pitfalls: Using `.unwrap()` on every `Result` in library code, turning recoverable errors into crashes.

quiz.q: In `fn load() -> Result<Config, AppError>`, what lets `std::fs::read_to_string(p)?` compile?
options: Nothing; ? only works with matching error types
quiz.explain: `?` calls `From::from` on the error, so it needs a `From<io::Error>` impl for `AppError`.

quiz.q: What does `?` do when applied to `Ok(v)`?
quiz.explain: On success `?` simply unwraps the value; it only returns early on `Err`.

concepts.name: Vectors
concepts.summary: Store a growable list in Vec<T>: create, push, index safely, iterate, and understand capacity.
concepts.why: Vec is the default collection in Rust; most data you process will pass through one.
concepts.body:
**`Vec<T>`** is a growable, heap-allocated array of `T`. Create one with `Vec::new()`, `Vec::with_capacity(n)` when you know roughly how many elements are coming, or the `vec![1, 2, 3]` macro.

Adding and removing: `push`, `pop` (returns `Option<T>`), `insert(i, x)`, `remove(i)` (shifts later elements, O(n)), `swap_remove(i)` (O(1), does not preserve order), `extend`, `truncate`, `clear`, `retain(|x| ...)` to filter in place, and `dedup` after a `sort`.

Reading: `v[i]` panics if out of bounds, while `v.get(i)` returns an `Option<&T>`. Use `get` when the index comes from outside your control.

Because a `Vec<T>` derefs to a slice `[T]`, every slice method is available: `len`, `is_empty`, `contains`, `iter`, `sort`, `sort_by_key`, `binary_search`, `windows`, `chunks`, `first`, `last`, `split_at`, and more. So you can pass `&v` wherever a `&[T]` is expected.

Iteration comes in three flavours:

- `for x in &v` borrows each element (`&T`),
- `for x in &mut v` gives `&mut T` for in-place edits,
- `for x in v` consumes the vector and yields owned `T`.

Under the hood a `Vec` is a pointer, a **length** and a **capacity**. When `len` reaches `capacity`, pushing reallocates (roughly doubling) and moves all elements. That is why the borrow checker forbids holding a reference into a vector across a `push`. `shrink_to_fit` releases spare capacity.

To store values of different types in one `Vec`, wrap them in an enum or use trait objects (covered later).
takeaways: Use `vec![]` or `Vec::with_capacity`; `get` returns `Option`, `[]` panics
A `Vec` derefs to a slice, so all slice methods apply
`&v`, `&mut v` and `v` in a `for` loop borrow, mutably borrow, or consume
pitfalls: Calling `remove(0)` repeatedly on a large Vec (O(n) each); use `VecDeque` for queue behaviour.

quiz.q: Why can't you keep `let first = &v[0];` alive across `v.push(9)`?
options: push may reallocate the buffer and leave `first` dangling
quiz.explain: Reallocation moves the elements, so the borrow checker forbids the overlapping shared and mutable borrows.

concepts.name: String and UTF-8 text
concepts.summary: Work with owned String and borrowed &str, build and format text, and handle UTF-8 correctly.
concepts.why: Text handling is where newcomers trip most, because Rust strings are always valid UTF-8 and never indexed by position.
concepts.body:
Rust has two main string types. **`String`** is an owned, growable, heap-allocated buffer. **`&str`** is a borrowed slice of UTF-8 text, from a `String` or a literal. Use `&str` for parameters, `String` when you need to own or build text. Convert with `s.as_str()` / `&s` one way and `s.to_string()`, `String::from(s)` or `s.to_owned()` the other.

Building text: `push_str`, `push` (one `char`), `+` (which takes the left `String` by value: `s1 + &s2`), and the `format!` macro, which is usually the clearest. `write!` into a `String` works too via `std::fmt::Write`.

Both types are guaranteed **valid UTF-8**. A character may take 1 to 4 bytes, so:

- `s.len()` is the length in **bytes**, not characters.
- `s[0]` does not compile. There is no O(1) way to get the n-th character.
- `s.chars()` iterates Unicode scalar values, `s.bytes()` iterates bytes, and `s.char_indices()` gives valid byte offsets for slicing.

Common operations: `trim`, `split`, `split_whitespace`, `lines`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `strip_prefix`, `replace`, `to_lowercase`, `parse::<T>()`, `repeat`, and `chars().rev().collect::<String>()` to reverse.

What users perceive as a character (a grapheme, e.g. an emoji with a skin-tone modifier) can be several `char`s; for that you need the `unicode-segmentation` crate.

Other string types exist for good reasons: `OsString`/`OsStr` for OS data that may not be UTF-8, `PathBuf`/`Path` for file paths, and `CString`/`CStr` for C interop. Do not force those through `String`.
takeaways: `String` owns text, `&str` borrows it; take `&str` parameters
`len()` counts bytes; iterate with `chars()` and slice at `char_indices` offsets
`format!` is the clearest way to build strings
pitfalls: Assuming `s.len()` is the number of characters for non-ASCII text.

quiz.q: What is `"héllo".len()`?
quiz.explain: `len` counts UTF-8 bytes and `é` takes two bytes, so the result is 6.

concepts.name: HashMap and the entry API
concepts.summary: Store key-value pairs in HashMap, update counts and groups with the entry API, and know when to use BTreeMap or HashSet.
concepts.why: Maps are the second most used collection, and the entry API is the idiomatic way to update them.
concepts.body:
**`HashMap<K, V>`** lives in `std::collections` (it is not in the prelude, so import it). Keys must implement `Eq` and `Hash`; deriving both on your own types is enough.

Basic operations: `insert(k, v)` returns the previous value as an `Option`; `get(&k)` returns `Option<&V>`; `get_mut`, `remove`, `contains_key`, `len`. You can build a map from an iterator of tuples with `.collect()` or from an array with `HashMap::from([(k, v), ...])`.

Inserting moves owned keys and values into the map. Lookups take a borrowed form, so a `HashMap<String, u32>` can be queried with a `&str`: `scores.get("ann")`.

The **entry API** handles "insert or update" in one lookup, avoiding the borrow-checker trouble of a `get` followed by `insert`:

- `*map.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;` counts occurrences.
- `map.entry(key).or_default().push(item);` groups items into `Vec`s.
- `or_insert_with(|| expensive())` computes the default lazily; `and_modify(|v| ...)` updates an existing value.

Iteration order of a `HashMap` is **unspecified** and changes between runs, because the default hasher (SipHash) is randomly seeded to resist denial-of-service attacks. If you need sorted keys, use **`BTreeMap`**, which keeps keys ordered and supports range queries. For raw speed on trusted keys, crates like `rustc-hash` or `ahash` provide faster hashers.

The companion sets are `HashSet<T>` and `BTreeSet<T>`, with `insert` returning `false` for duplicates and set operations like `intersection` and `union`. `VecDeque` (a ring buffer queue) and `BinaryHeap` (a priority queue) round out the standard collections.
takeaways: Import `HashMap` from `std::collections`; keys need `Eq + Hash`
Use `entry().or_insert()` / `or_default()` for counting and grouping
HashMap order is random; use `BTreeMap` when order matters
pitfalls: Relying on HashMap iteration order in output or tests.

quiz.q: What is the idiomatic way to increment a counter for `word` in a `HashMap<String, u32>`?
quiz.explain: The entry API finds or creates the slot in one lookup and gives a `&mut u32` to increment.

concepts.name: Modules, crates and packages
concepts.summary: Organise code into modules and files, control visibility with pub, and add dependencies in Cargo.toml.
concepts.why: Every project beyond one file needs modules, and every real project depends on crates from crates.io.
concepts.body:
A **package** is what `cargo new` creates: a `Cargo.toml` plus one or more **crates**. A crate is a compilation unit, either a binary (rooted at `src/main.rs`) or a library (rooted at `src/lib.rs`). A package can have both; the binary then uses the library by its package name.

Inside a crate, code is organised into a tree of **modules**. `mod parser;` in `main.rs` or `lib.rs` tells the compiler to load `src/parser.rs` (or `src/parser/mod.rs`). Submodules of `parser` live in `src/parser/`. You can also write a module inline: `mod tests { ... }`.

Everything is **private by default** to its module (and that module's children). Mark items `pub` to expose them; `pub(crate)` exposes within the crate only. For structs, each field needs its own `pub`; for enums, making the enum `pub` makes all variants public.

Paths: `crate::parser::parse` is absolute from the crate root, `super::` goes up one level, `self::` is the current module. `use` brings names into scope; idiomatic style imports the parent module for functions (`use std::fs;` then `fs::read`) and the item itself for types (`use std::collections::HashMap;`). `pub use` re-exports, letting you present a flatter public API than your file layout.

**Dependencies** go in `Cargo.toml` under `[dependencies]`, e.g. `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }`, or simply run `cargo add serde --features derive`. Version requirements are semver ranges: `"1.4"` means at least 1.4.0 and below 2.0.0. `Cargo.lock` records exact versions; commit it for applications. `[dev-dependencies]` are only for tests and examples. Large projects group crates in a **workspace** sharing one lock file and `target/` directory.
takeaways: A package holds crates; a crate is a tree of modules rooted at main.rs or lib.rs
Items and struct fields are private unless marked `pub`
`cargo add` and `[dependencies]` pull crates from crates.io using semver ranges
pitfalls: Writing `mod foo;` in every file that uses `foo`; declare a module once, then `use` it elsewhere.

quiz.q: A struct is `pub` but its fields are not. What can code in another module do?
options: Construct it with a struct literal
Use it, but not access or set its private fields directly
Nothing; the struct is still private
quiz.explain: Field privacy is separate from type privacy, so outside code needs public methods such as `new` to create or inspect it.

quiz.q: What does the dependency requirement `rand = "0.8.5"` allow?
quiz.explain: Cargo's caret semantics treat the leftmost non-zero component as the major version, so 0.8.x upgrades are allowed but not 0.9.

concepts.name: Traits
concepts.summary: Define shared behaviour with traits, implement them for your types, and use default methods and impl Trait parameters.
concepts.why: Traits are Rust's mechanism for polymorphism and code reuse; the whole standard library is built on them.
concepts.body:
A **trait** declares a set of methods that types can implement, similar to an interface. You write `trait Summary { fn summarize(&self) -> String; }` and then `impl Summary for Article { ... }` for each type.

Traits can provide **default methods** that implementors get for free and may override. A default method can call the required ones, so a trait can ask for one small method and offer many on top. This is exactly how `Iterator` works: implement `next`, and you get `map`, `filter`, `sum` and dozens more.

To accept "anything that implements `Summary`", the simplest syntax is `fn notify(item: &impl Summary)`. In return position, `fn make() -> impl Summary` returns some concrete type the caller cannot name. Both are resolved at compile time, with no runtime cost.

The **orphan rule** says you can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. You can implement your trait for `Vec<T>`, or `Display` for your struct, but not `Display` for `Vec<T>`. The usual workaround is a newtype wrapper.

Traits can require other traits (**supertraits**): `trait Pretty: std::fmt::Display { ... }` means implementors must also implement `Display`, and default methods may use `to_string()`.

To call a trait method, the trait must be in scope. If `x.summarize()` mysteriously fails with "method not found", you probably forgot `use crate::Summary;`. Many crates provide a `prelude` module for this reason.

Since Rust 1.75, traits can contain `async fn` and `-> impl Trait` methods too.
takeaways: A trait lists required methods and may supply default ones
`&impl Trait` parameters and `-> impl Trait` returns are static and zero-cost
Orphan rule: you own the trait or the type; bring traits into scope to call their methods
pitfalls: Forgetting to `use` a trait and wondering why its method does not exist.

quiz.q: Which impl is forbidden by the orphan rule in your own crate?
quiz.explain: Both `Display` and `Vec` come from the standard library, so neither is local to your crate.

concepts.name: Generics and trait bounds
concepts.summary: Write functions and types over any T, constrain T with trait bounds and where clauses, and know what monomorphization costs.
concepts.why: Generics let one piece of code work for many types with no runtime overhead, and you read them in every API signature.
concepts.body:
**Generics** let you write code once for many types. `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(items: &[T]) -> &T` works for slices of integers, floats or strings. Structs and enums can be generic too: `struct Pair<T> { a: T, b: T }`, and of course `Vec<T>`, `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>`.

Inside a generic function you can only do what the **trait bounds** promise. Without `T: PartialOrd` you cannot compare with `>`; without `T: Clone` you cannot call `.clone()`. The compiler checks the generic body once against the bounds, so errors appear at the definition, not deep inside an instantiation.

Bounds can be written inline (`T: Display + Clone`) or in a **`where` clause**, which reads better when there are several:

```rust
fn report<K, V>(map: &HashMap<K, V>) where K: Display + Eq + Hash, V: Debug { }
```

`impl` blocks can be generic (`impl<T> Pair<T> { }`) or conditional: `impl<T: Display> Pair<T> { fn show(&self) }` adds methods only when `T` qualifies. A **blanket impl** like `impl<T: Display> ToString for T` gives a trait to every type meeting a bound.

Rust compiles generics by **monomorphization**: it generates a specialised copy for each concrete type used. That makes them as fast as hand-written code, at the cost of compile time and binary size. When that matters, or when you need a collection of mixed types, trait objects (`dyn Trait`, a later lesson) trade a little runtime speed for one shared copy.

`impl Trait` in argument position is shorthand for an anonymous generic parameter. Use a named `T` when you need to mention the type twice or let callers specify it with turbofish syntax: `parse::<u32>()`, `collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

Generics also accept **const parameters**: `fn first<T, const N: usize>(arr: [T; N])`.
takeaways: Trait bounds define what a generic body is allowed to do with `T`
Use `where` clauses for long bounds; conditional `impl` blocks add methods per bound
Generics are monomorphized: zero runtime cost, more compile time and code size
pitfalls: Adding bounds to a struct definition instead of only to the impl blocks that need them.

quiz.q: Why does `fn max<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T { if a > b { a } else { b } }` fail to compile?
options: a and b are moved twice
T has no PartialOrd bound, so `>` is not known to exist
quiz.explain: Generic bodies may only use operations guaranteed by bounds; comparison needs `T: PartialOrd`.

concepts.name: Derive and the standard traits
concepts.summary: Know Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Ord, Default, Display and From/Into, and when to derive or implement them.
concepts.why: These traits decide whether your types can be printed, compared, hashed, copied or converted, so every type you write needs the right set.
concepts.body:
The standard library defines a set of traits that nearly every type should consider. Most can be generated with **`#[derive(...)]`**, which implements them field by field (so each field must implement the trait too).

- `Debug`: `{:?}` formatting for developers. Derive it on almost everything.
- `Clone`: explicit `.clone()`. `Copy`: implicit bitwise copy on assignment; only for small types whose fields are all `Copy`, and it requires `Clone`.
- `PartialEq`/`Eq`: `==`. `Eq` promises equality is reflexive, which floats break (`NaN != NaN`), so `f64` is only `PartialEq`.
- `PartialOrd`/`Ord`: `<`, sorting, `max`. Derived ordering compares fields in declaration order, and enum variants in declaration order.
- `Hash`: needed for `HashMap` keys, together with `Eq`. Keep it consistent with `PartialEq`: equal values must hash equally.
- `Default`: `T::default()` and `..Default::default()` in struct literals. Enums can derive it by marking one variant `#[default]`.

Some must be written by hand:

- **`Display`**: user-facing `{}` formatting. Implement `fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result` using `write!`. It also gives you `.to_string()` for free.
- **`From<T>`**: infallible conversion. Implementing `From<A> for B` automatically provides `Into<B> for A`, so implement `From` and accept `impl Into<B>` in APIs when convenient. `TryFrom` is the fallible version.

Other traits you will see in signatures: `AsRef<str>` (cheap reference conversion), `Deref`, `Drop` (custom cleanup when a value goes out of scope), `Iterator` and `IntoIterator`, `Send`/`Sync` for threads, and `FromStr`, which powers `str::parse`.
takeaways: Derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq` (and friends) unless you have a reason not to
`Copy` only for small plain-data types; `Eq` and `Hash` must agree with `PartialEq`
Implement `Display` for user-facing output and `From` for conversions; you get `to_string` and `Into` free
pitfalls: Implementing `Into` directly instead of `From`, which loses the blanket conversion.

quiz.q: Why can't you derive `Eq` on a struct containing an `f64` field?
options: f64 does not implement Eq because NaN != NaN
Eq cannot be derived at all
quiz.explain: `Eq` requires reflexive equality, which floating-point NaN violates, so `f64` only implements `PartialEq`.

quiz.q: You implement `From<Celsius> for Kelvin`. What else do you get automatically?
quiz.explain: A blanket impl in std provides `Into<U> for T` whenever `U: From<T>`.

concepts.name: Closures
concepts.summary: Write anonymous functions that capture their environment, understand Fn, FnMut and FnOnce, and use move closures.
concepts.why: Closures power iterators, callbacks, threads and async code, and their capture rules follow directly from ownership.
concepts.body:
A **closure** is an anonymous function that can capture variables from the scope where it is defined: `let add = |a, b| a + b;` or with a block body `|x: i32| -> i32 { x * factor }`. Parameter and return types are usually inferred from the first use.

Closures capture in the least demanding way their body allows: by shared reference if they only read a variable, by mutable reference if they modify it, or by value if they move it out. Borrowing rules apply to those captures, so a closure holding `&mut count` blocks other uses of `count` while it is alive.

The capture mode decides which **Fn trait** the closure implements:

- `FnOnce`: can be called at least once; it may consume captured values. Every closure implements it.
- `FnMut`: can be called repeatedly and may mutate captures.
- `Fn`: can be called repeatedly through a shared reference; it only reads captures.

APIs take the most permissive bound that works for them: `Option::map` takes `FnOnce` because it calls once, `Iterator::for_each` takes `FnMut`, and things called concurrently or many times through `&` take `Fn`.

The **`move`** keyword forces captures by value, even if the body only reads them. You need it when the closure outlives the current scope: returning a closure, spawning a thread, or passing it into async tasks. Moving a `Copy` value copies it; to move a clone and keep the original, clone into a new variable first.

To accept a closure, use generics (`fn apply<F: Fn(i32) -> i32>(f: F)`), and to return one, `-> impl Fn(i32) -> i32`. When you need to store closures of different types together, box them: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(i32) -> i32>>`. Plain `fn` items also implement all three traits, so you can pass a function name wherever a closure is expected.
takeaways: Closures capture by reference, mutable reference or value, as needed by the body
`Fn` ⊂ `FnMut` ⊂ `FnOnce`: callers ask for the weakest bound they can
Use `move` when the closure must outlive the scope that created it
pitfalls: Forgetting `move` on a closure passed to `thread::spawn` and getting a 'may outlive borrowed value' error.

quiz.q: A closure pushes into a captured `Vec`. Which is the most specific trait it implements?
quiz.explain: Mutating a capture requires a mutable borrow, so the closure is `FnMut` (and therefore also `FnOnce`) but not `Fn`.

concepts.name: Iterators
concepts.summary: Chain lazy iterator adapters like map, filter and enumerate, finish with collect, sum or fold, and implement Iterator.
concepts.why: Iterator chains are the idiomatic way to process collections in Rust and compile to code as fast as hand-written loops.
concepts.body:
An **iterator** is anything implementing `trait Iterator { type Item; fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>; }`. Each call to `next` yields `Some(item)` until it returns `None`. `Item` is an **associated type**: each iterator has exactly one item type.

Collections give you three iterators: `iter()` yields `&T`, `iter_mut()` yields `&mut T`, and `into_iter()` yields owned `T`, consuming the collection. A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in &v` yields references.

**Adapters** turn an iterator into another iterator: `map`, `filter`, `filter_map`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `chain`, `take`, `skip`, `take_while`, `flat_map`, `rev`, `peekable`, `windows` on slices. Adapters are **lazy**: nothing happens until a consumer pulls items. A `map` with no consumer does nothing (and the compiler warns).

**Consumers** drive the iteration: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `min`/`max`, `max_by_key`, `fold`, `any`, `all`, `find`, `position`, `for_each`, `last`.

`collect` is generic over its output: it can build a `Vec`, `String`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, and even a `Result<Vec<T>, E>` from an iterator of `Result`s, stopping at the first error. Tell it what you want with a type annotation or turbofish: `collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

Thanks to inlining, iterator chains usually compile to the same machine code as a manual loop, and they often avoid bounds checks. Prefer them for transforming data; use a plain `for` loop when the body has complex control flow or side effects.

To make your own type iterable, implement `next`; all adapters come with the trait. Implement `IntoIterator` for your collection so it works in `for` loops.
takeaways: Implement `next` and you get every adapter for free
Adapters are lazy; consumers like `collect`, `sum` and `for` drive them
`collect` can build any `FromIterator` type, including `Result<Vec<_>, E>`
pitfalls: Calling `.map(...)` for side effects without a consumer, so nothing runs.

quiz.q: What does `v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}"));` print?
options: Nothing, because the iterator is never consumed
quiz.explain: Adapters are lazy; without a consumer such as `for_each` or `collect`, the closure never runs (the compiler warns).

quiz.q: Which call yields owned `String`s from a `Vec<String>` and consumes the vector?
quiz.explain: `into_iter()` on an owned `Vec` takes ownership and yields its elements by value.

concepts.name: Lifetime annotations
concepts.summary: Read and write lifetime parameters like 'a that tell the compiler how returned references relate to inputs.
concepts.why: Lifetimes appear in signatures as soon as a function returns a reference or a struct holds one.
concepts.body:
Every reference has a **lifetime**: the region of code during which it is valid. Usually the compiler infers them. Annotations are needed when a function's signature alone does not say which input a returned reference comes from.

```rust
fn longer<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str
```

reads as: "for some lifetime `'a`, both inputs live at least as long as `'a`, and the result is valid for `'a`". In practice the result is valid only as long as the shorter of the two inputs. Annotations never change how long anything lives; they describe relationships so the borrow checker can verify callers.

You rarely write them, thanks to the **elision rules**:

- Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime.
- If there is exactly one input lifetime, it is assigned to all output references.
- In methods with `&self` or `&mut self`, outputs get the lifetime of `self`.

So `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` needs nothing, but `longer` above does, because there are two inputs and no `self`.

A struct that holds a reference must declare a lifetime parameter: `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }`. A `Parser` then cannot outlive the string it reads. In `impl<'a> Parser<'a>` you can return `&'a str` slices that stay valid even after the parser itself is dropped.

`'static` means "valid for the whole program": string literals are `&'static str`. Seeing a compiler suggestion to add `'static` is usually a hint that you should return an owned value instead.

When fighting lifetimes in your own structs, ask whether the struct should simply own its data (`String` instead of `&str`). Borrowing structs are great for short-lived views and parsers, not for long-lived state.
takeaways: Lifetime annotations describe relationships between references; they never extend a value's life
Elision covers single-input and `&self` methods; otherwise annotate
Structs holding references need `<'a>` and cannot outlive the borrowed data
pitfalls: Annotating `-> &'static str` to silence an error, when returning an owned `String` is the real fix.

quiz.q: Why does `fn pick(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str` need an explicit lifetime?
options: There are two input references and no self, so elision cannot pick one
Return types can never be references
It does not; it compiles as is
quiz.explain: With multiple input lifetimes and no `self`, the elision rules do not assign an output lifetime.

concepts.name: Testing
concepts.summary: Write unit tests with #[test] and assert macros, integration tests in tests/, doc tests, and run them with cargo test.
concepts.why: Rust ships testing in the toolchain, and well-tested crates are the norm in the ecosystem.
concepts.body:
A **test** is a function annotated `#[test]`. It passes if it returns normally and fails if it panics. Assertions are macros: `assert!(cond)`, `assert_eq!(left, right)`, `assert_ne!`, each with optional format arguments for a custom message. `assert_eq!` prints both values on failure, so the compared types must implement `Debug` and `PartialEq`.

**Unit tests** conventionally live in the same file as the code, in a child module:

```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn works() { assert_eq!(add(2, 2), 4); }
}
```

`#[cfg(test)]` compiles the module only for `cargo test`, and because it is a child module it can test private functions.

**Integration tests** go in the `tests/` directory. Each file there is a separate crate that uses your library like an external user would, through its public API only.

**Doc tests**: code blocks in `///` documentation comments are compiled and run by `cargo test`, which keeps examples in your docs honest.

Other tools:

- A test can return `Result<(), E>` and use `?`; returning `Err` fails it.
- `#[should_panic(expected = "divide by zero")]` asserts a panic with matching message.
- `#[ignore]` skips slow tests unless you run `cargo test -- --ignored`.
- `cargo test parse` runs only tests whose names contain `parse`; `cargo test -- --nocapture` shows `println!` output.

Tests run in parallel threads by default, so tests that touch shared state like files or environment variables need unique paths or `--test-threads=1`. Popular additions include `proptest` for property testing and `insta` for snapshot tests.
takeaways: `#[test]` functions pass unless they panic; use `assert_eq!` for good failure output
Unit tests sit in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` and can reach private items
`tests/` holds integration tests; `///` examples run as doc tests
pitfalls: Tests that share a temp file or env var and fail randomly because tests run in parallel.

quiz.q: Where should a test go that should only exercise your crate's public API?
quiz.explain: Each file in `tests/` is compiled as a separate crate, so it can only use public items.

concepts.name: Box, Rc and RefCell
concepts.summary: Put values on the heap with Box, share ownership with Rc, and mutate shared data with RefCell.
concepts.why: Recursive types, shared graphs and trees, and trait objects all need smart pointers beyond plain references.
concepts.body:
A **smart pointer** is a struct that owns data and acts like a pointer by implementing `Deref` (so `*p` and method calls reach the inner value) and `Drop` (cleanup when it goes away). `String` and `Vec` are smart pointers too.

**`Box<T>`** stores a `T` on the heap with a single owner. Use it for:

- recursive types, whose size would otherwise be infinite: `enum List { Cons(i32, Box<List>), Nil }`,
- trait objects: `Box<dyn Error>`, `Box<dyn Fn()>`,
- moving a large value around cheaply by moving only the pointer.

**`Rc<T>`** (reference counted) allows **multiple owners** of the same value in single-threaded code. `Rc::clone(&rc)` increments a counter instead of copying the data, and the value is dropped when the last `Rc` goes away. `Rc::strong_count` shows the count. Data inside an `Rc` is read-only, because shared ownership implies shared references.

**`RefCell<T>`** moves the borrowing rules from compile time to runtime. `cell.borrow()` returns a guard acting like `&T`, `cell.borrow_mut()` one acting like `&mut T`, and violating "many readers or one writer" **panics** instead of failing to compile. `try_borrow_mut` returns a `Result` instead.

Combined, **`Rc<RefCell<T>>`** gives shared, mutable data: a common shape for graphs, observers and GUI state. Use it sparingly; it is a sign that ownership is genuinely shared, not a way around thinking about ownership.

Two reference-counted values pointing at each other never reach a count of zero, which **leaks** memory. Break cycles with **`Weak<T>`** (`Rc::downgrade`), a non-owning pointer you `upgrade()` to an `Option<Rc<T>>`, typically for parent links in trees.

`Rc` and `RefCell` are not thread-safe; their multithreaded counterparts are `Arc` and `Mutex`.
takeaways: `Box<T>`: single owner on the heap, for recursive types and trait objects
`Rc<T>`: shared ownership via reference counting, read-only, single thread
`RefCell<T>`: borrow rules checked at runtime (panics on violation); break `Rc` cycles with `Weak`
pitfalls: Holding a `borrow()` guard while calling code that does `borrow_mut()` on the same cell, which panics.

quiz.q: What happens if you call `cell.borrow_mut()` while a `cell.borrow()` guard is still alive?
options: It waits until the guard is dropped
The program panics with a BorrowMutError
quiz.explain: `RefCell` enforces the borrow rules at runtime and panics when they are broken.

quiz.q: Two `Rc` nodes point to each other. What happens when all outside handles are dropped?
options: Rust detects the cycle and frees them
The memory leaks because each count stays at 1
quiz.explain: Reference counting cannot collect cycles; one direction should use `Weak` instead.

concepts.name: Lifetimes in depth
concepts.summary: Outlives bounds, what T: 'static really means, higher-ranked bounds, and how impl Trait captures lifetimes in Rust 2024.
concepts.why: Library signatures, thread and task spawning, and callback APIs all hinge on these less obvious lifetime rules.
concepts.body:
Lifetimes form a hierarchy: `'b: 'a` ("`'b` outlives `'a`") means anything valid for `'b` is valid for `'a`, so a `&'static str` can be used where a `&'a str` is expected. The same syntax applies to types: **`T: 'a`** means every reference inside `T` lives at least as long as `'a`.

**`T: 'static`** is the most misread bound. It does not mean the value lives forever. It means `T` contains no borrowed data shorter than `'static`, so the holder may keep it as long as it likes. `String`, `Vec<u8>` and `Arc<Mutex<X>>` are all `'static` types even though they are dropped normally. `thread::spawn` and `tokio::spawn` require `F: 'static` because the task may outlive the caller's stack frame; that is why you `move` owned data in rather than borrowing locals.

**Higher-ranked trait bounds** say "for every lifetime": `F: for<'x> Fn(&'x str) -> &'x str` accepts a closure that works on input of any lifetime, rather than one chosen by the caller. You mostly see them implicitly, since `Fn(&str) -> &str` is sugar for exactly that.

Reborrowing is why passing a `&mut T` to a function does not move it: the compiler inserts `&mut *r`, a shorter borrow, and you can use `r` again afterwards.

In the **2024 edition**, a return-position `impl Trait` automatically captures every generic parameter and lifetime in scope. When a returned iterator should not be tied to some input, opt out with **precise capturing**: `fn ids(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> + use<>` (or list exactly which parameters it uses, e.g. `use<'a, T>`).

Finally, trait object lifetimes have defaults: `Box<dyn Trait>` means `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`, while `&'a dyn Trait` means `&'a (dyn Trait + 'a)`. Write `Box<dyn Trait + 'a>` to store borrowing objects.
takeaways: `T: 'static` means 'owns its data', not 'lives forever'
`for<'x>` bounds accept callbacks that work for any input lifetime
Rust 2024 `impl Trait` returns capture all lifetimes; narrow with `use<..>`
`Box<dyn Trait>` defaults to `+ 'static`
pitfalls: Trying to satisfy `'static` by leaking or making data global, when cloning or `Arc` would do.

quiz.q: Which of these types satisfies `T: 'static`?
quiz.explain: `String` owns its contents and holds no non-static references, so it meets the bound even though it is dropped normally.

quiz.q: In Rust 2024, what does `-> impl Iterator<Item = u8> + use<>` on a `&self` method say?
options: The returned type captures no generic or lifetime parameters
quiz.explain: `use<>` is precise capturing with an empty list, so the hidden type cannot depend on `self`'s lifetime.

concepts.name: Trait objects and dyn
concepts.summary: Use dyn Trait for runtime polymorphism, understand vtables and fat pointers, and know the dyn-compatibility rules.
concepts.why: Plugin systems, heterogeneous collections and error boxes need dynamic dispatch rather than generics.
concepts.body:
Generics pick the concrete type at compile time. A **trait object**, `dyn Trait`, picks it at runtime. Because the size of the underlying type is unknown, a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Draw`, `Box<dyn Draw>`, `Rc<dyn Draw>` or `Arc<dyn Draw + Send + Sync>`.

Such a pointer is a **fat pointer**: two words, one pointing to the data and one to a **vtable**, a static table holding the concrete type's method pointers plus its size, alignment and drop function. Calling a method is an indirect call through the vtable. That costs a little (mostly by blocking inlining), but you get one compiled copy of the calling code and can mix types in one collection: `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>`.

Not every trait can be a trait object. A trait is **dyn compatible** (formerly "object safe") only if its methods could be called through a vtable, which rules out:

- generic methods (`fn visit<T>(&self, t: T)`), since the vtable cannot hold infinitely many instantiations,
- methods that mention `Self` outside the receiver, such as returning `Self`,
- associated constants, and static functions without `self`.

You can keep such methods on an otherwise compatible trait by adding `where Self: Sized`, which excludes them from the vtable. `Clone` is not dyn compatible, so cloning boxed objects needs a helper method like `fn box_clone(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape>`.

Since Rust 1.86, **trait upcasting** works: if `trait Shape: Debug`, a `&dyn Shape` coerces to `&dyn Debug`. To get back the concrete type, use `std::any::Any` and `downcast_ref::<T>()`.

Rule of thumb: generics by default; `dyn` when you need a heterogeneous collection, want to reduce compile time or binary size, or need to choose implementations at runtime.
takeaways: `dyn Trait` lives behind a pointer that carries a vtable: one copy of code, indirect calls
Generic methods and `Self`-returning methods break dyn compatibility unless `where Self: Sized`
Use `dyn` for heterogeneous collections and runtime choice; generics otherwise
pitfalls: Defaulting to `Box<dyn Trait>` everywhere out of habit from OOP languages, where generics would be simpler and faster.

quiz.q: Why can't `trait Visitor { fn visit<T: Debug>(&self, t: T); }` be used as `dyn Visitor`?
options: Traits with Debug bounds are never dyn compatible
dyn requires all methods to take self by value
A vtable cannot contain an entry for every possible T
quiz.explain: Generic methods would need one vtable entry per instantiation, so they make the trait dyn incompatible.

quiz.q: What is stored in a `&dyn Shape` reference?
options: A pointer to the data and a pointer to a vtable
Only a pointer to the data
A type ID and the value
quiz.explain: Trait object references are fat pointers combining the data pointer with the concrete type's vtable.

concepts.name: Custom errors, thiserror and anyhow
concepts.summary: Design error types with std::error::Error, derive them with thiserror in libraries, and add context with anyhow in applications.
concepts.why: Good error types make failures diagnosable; the thiserror/anyhow split is the ecosystem's standard pattern.
concepts.body:
A proper error type implements **`std::error::Error`**, which requires `Debug` and `Display`, and optionally provides `source()` to expose the underlying cause. Callers can then print it, box it as `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>`, and walk the chain of causes.

For a **library**, define an enum of the failures callers might want to react to:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum ConfigError {
    #[error("cannot read {path}")]
    Io { path: String, #[source] source: std::io::Error },
    #[error("invalid port {0}")]
    BadPort(u32),
    #[error(transparent)]
    Parse(#[from] std::num::ParseIntError),
}
```

The **thiserror** derive writes the `Display`, `Error::source` and `From` impls you would otherwise write by hand; it adds nothing to your public API. Keep variants meaningful: callers match on them.

For an **application**, you usually just want to report what went wrong with enough context. **anyhow** provides `anyhow::Result<T>` (with an `anyhow::Error` that wraps any error), `.context("loading config")` and `.with_context(|| format!(...))` on both `Result` and `Option`, plus `bail!` and `ensure!` macros. Printing with `{:#}` shows the whole cause chain on one line, and `{:?}` adds a backtrace when `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`.

Guidelines that hold up:

- Do not put the source error's message into your own `Display` and also return it from `source()`, or reporters print it twice.
- Make library errors `Send + Sync + 'static` so they work across threads and async tasks.
- Mark public error enums `#[non_exhaustive]` if you may add variants later.
- Libraries should not depend on anyhow in their public API; applications can freely mix both.

The example below implements the same pattern without crates, so you can see what the derive generates.
takeaways: Error types implement `Debug + Display + Error`, exposing causes via `source()`
Libraries: specific enums, often derived with thiserror
Applications: anyhow with `.context()` for readable chains
pitfalls: Returning `Result<T, String>` from libraries, which callers cannot match on or chain.

quiz.q: Which crate split is the common convention?
options: anyhow in libraries, thiserror in applications
thiserror for library error types, anyhow in applications
quiz.explain: Libraries expose precise matchable types (thiserror), while applications mostly report errors with context (anyhow).

concepts.name: Interior mutability: Cell, OnceCell, LazyLock
concepts.summary: Mutate through shared references safely with Cell, RefCell, OnceCell and LazyLock, and see how UnsafeCell underpins them all.
concepts.why: Caches, counters, lazy globals and shared state all rely on interior mutability, and choosing the right cell avoids panics and locks.
concepts.body:
Normally `&T` means "read-only". **Interior mutability** is the controlled exception: types that allow mutation through a shared reference by enforcing safety some other way. They all build on **`UnsafeCell<T>`**, the only legal way in Rust to mutate data reachable through `&`; every other approach is undefined behaviour.

Single-threaded cells (not `Sync`):

- **`Cell<T>`**: no borrowing at all. You `get` a copy (for `Copy` types), `set`, `replace` or `take` the whole value. Zero overhead, can never panic. Ideal for counters and flags.
- **`RefCell<T>`**: hands out `Ref`/`RefMut` guards and tracks borrows at runtime, panicking on conflicts. Use when you need references into the value.
- **`OnceCell<T>`**: written at most once; `get_or_init(|| ...)` computes on first use. Good for lazily computed fields.
- **`LazyCell<T, F>`**: an `OnceCell` bundled with its initializer.

Thread-safe equivalents:

- **`OnceLock<T>`** (since 1.70) and **`LazyLock<T>`** (since 1.80) for lazily initialised globals: `static CONFIG: LazyLock<Config> = LazyLock::new(load);`. They replace the `lazy_static` and `once_cell` crates.
- **atomics** (`AtomicUsize`, `AtomicBool`) are the thread-safe `Cell` for integers.
- **`Mutex<T>`/`RwLock<T>`** are the thread-safe `RefCell`: they block instead of panicking.

Avoid `static mut`: in the 2024 edition, taking a reference to one is denied by default (the `static_mut_refs` lint), because it invites data races and aliasing bugs. Use an atomic, a `Mutex`, or a `LazyLock` instead.

Interior mutability is a tool for caches, memoization, reference-counted graphs and statistics behind `&self` APIs. If you can restructure so that one owner holds `&mut`, that is usually simpler.
takeaways: All interior mutability is built on `UnsafeCell`
`Cell` for small `Copy` values, `RefCell` for borrowed access, `OnceCell` for compute-once
Use `LazyLock`/`OnceLock`, atomics or `Mutex` for globals; avoid `static mut`
pitfalls: Using `RefCell` where `Cell` would do and paying for (and risking) runtime borrow panics.

quiz.q: You need a lazily initialised global configuration readable from many threads. What fits best?
quiz.explain: `LazyLock` is thread-safe, initialises once on first access, and needs no unsafe code.

concepts.name: Threads and scoped threads
concepts.summary: Spawn OS threads, move data into them, join their results, and borrow local data safely with thread::scope.
concepts.why: Threads are the foundation of parallelism in Rust, and the type system is what makes them free of data races.
concepts.body:
`std::thread::spawn` starts an OS thread running a closure and returns a `JoinHandle<T>`. Calling `join()` waits for it and returns `Result<T, _>`: `Ok` with the closure's return value, or `Err` if the thread panicked. A panic in a spawned thread does not crash the main thread by itself.

The closure must be `Send + 'static`. `'static` because the new thread could outlive the function that spawned it, so it cannot borrow the caller's locals; `Send` because its captured values move to another thread. Hence the usual pattern: a `move` closure that takes ownership of what it needs, cloning or wrapping in `Arc` anything shared.

Since Rust 1.63, **scoped threads** remove the `'static` requirement when threads finish before the function returns:

```rust
std::thread::scope(|s| {
    s.spawn(|| work(&data[..half]));
    s.spawn(|| work(&data[half..]));
}); // all scoped threads are joined here
```

The scope guarantees every thread is joined before it ends, so borrowing local data is safe, and the usual borrow rules still prevent two threads from mutating the same thing.

This is where Rust's slogan "fearless concurrency" comes from: sharing data between threads without synchronisation is a compile error, not a heisenbug. Data races are impossible in safe Rust, although deadlocks and logic races still are.

Practical notes:

- `std::thread::available_parallelism()` tells you how many threads make sense.
- OS threads are relatively heavy (each has its own stack, by default 2 MiB for spawned threads). For thousands of concurrent I/O tasks use async; for CPU-bound data parallelism, the **rayon** crate turns `iter()` into `par_iter()` with a work-stealing pool.
- `thread::Builder` sets names and stack sizes; `thread::sleep` pauses the current thread.
takeaways: `thread::spawn` needs a `Send + 'static` closure, so `move` owned data in
`join()` returns the result, or `Err` if the thread panicked
`thread::scope` lets threads borrow local data because they are joined before it returns
pitfalls: Spawning a thread per small task; use a pool (rayon) or async for many tiny units of work.

quiz.q: Why can a closure passed to `thread::scope`'s `s.spawn` borrow a local Vec, but one passed to `thread::spawn` cannot?
options: The scope joins all its threads before returning, so borrows cannot outlive the data
thread::spawn runs on the same thread
Scoped threads are not real OS threads
quiz.explain: Because the scope guarantees completion before it ends, the borrow checker can verify the borrows; plain `spawn` requires `'static`.

concepts.name: Arc, Mutex and RwLock
concepts.summary: Share data across threads with Arc, guard mutation with Mutex or RwLock, use atomics for counters, and avoid deadlocks.
concepts.why: Any multithreaded server or worker pool shares some state, and these are the standard building blocks.
concepts.body:
To share ownership across threads you need **`Arc<T>`** (atomically reference counted), the thread-safe version of `Rc`. Cloning an `Arc` bumps an atomic counter; the data is read-only through it.

To mutate shared data, wrap it in a lock: **`Arc<Mutex<T>>`**. `mutex.lock()` blocks until it gets exclusive access and returns a `MutexGuard`, which derefs to `&mut T` and **unlocks when dropped**. There is no separate `unlock` call to forget; keep critical sections short by limiting the guard's scope with a block or an explicit `drop(guard)`.

`lock()` returns a `Result` because of **poisoning**: if a thread panics while holding the guard, the mutex is marked poisoned, since the data might be half-updated. Most code calls `.unwrap()` (propagating the panic) or recovers with `.unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`.

**`RwLock<T>`** allows many readers (`read()`) or one writer (`write()`); it helps when reads dominate and are long. For short critical sections a `Mutex` is often faster.

For simple counters and flags, **atomics** like `AtomicU64` avoid locks entirely: `counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)`. Memory orderings beyond `Relaxed` (`Acquire`/`Release`, `SeqCst`) matter when the atomic guards other data; if unsure, use `SeqCst` or a `Mutex`.

Deadlocks are still possible: two threads taking locks A then B and B then A. Always acquire multiple locks in a fixed order, and never call unknown code (callbacks) while holding a lock. A guard held across a call that tries to lock the same `Mutex` again deadlocks the thread with itself; std mutexes are not reentrant.

Alternatives: `parking_lot` offers smaller, faster locks without poisoning; channels avoid shared state altogether.
takeaways: `Arc` shares ownership across threads; `Mutex`/`RwLock` add mutation
Guards unlock on drop; keep them in the smallest possible scope
Use atomics for counters and a fixed lock order to avoid deadlocks
pitfalls: Locking a `Mutex` twice on the same thread (for example in a helper called while holding the guard), which deadlocks.

quiz.q: What happens to a std `Mutex` if a thread panics while holding its guard?
options: The data is reset to default
Nothing; the guard is just dropped
The mutex becomes poisoned and later lock() calls return Err
quiz.explain: Poisoning signals the data may be inconsistent; `lock()` then returns `Err(PoisonError)`, from which you can still recover the guard.

quiz.q: Why is `Rc<RefCell<T>>` rejected by `thread::spawn` while `Arc<Mutex<T>>` is accepted?
options: Rc's counter and RefCell's borrow flag are not thread-safe, so they are not Send/Sync
quiz.explain: Non-atomic reference counts and borrow flags would race, so those types do not implement `Send`/`Sync`.

concepts.name: Message passing with channels
concepts.summary: Send values between threads with mpsc channels, use bounded channels for backpressure, and shut down cleanly.
concepts.why: Channels let threads cooperate by passing ownership instead of sharing memory, which is often simpler and safer.
concepts.body:
A **channel** moves values from producers to a consumer. `std::sync::mpsc::channel()` returns a `(Sender<T>, Receiver<T>)` pair; mpsc stands for multiple producer, single consumer. Clone the `Sender` to give one to each producer thread.
